Neonates of the Crested gecko (Correlophus ciliatus) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that is highly dependent on thermal conditions. When eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], hatching typically occurs after approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days], although incubation periods can range from 60 to 150 days depending on minor thermal fluctuations and individual variation. At the moment of eclosion, these newly emerged hatchlings possess a modest wet weight at birth of roughly 1.25 grams [Wwb = roughly 1.25 grams]. This small initial mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the species, wherein the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. Following first prey capture and the trophic switch to active feeding, the hatchling enters a prolonged juvenile phase characterized by rapid somatic growth. This initial mass is a critical baseline for assessing subsequent developmental trajectories.

Female Crested geckos attain a considerably larger body size compared to males, with the ultimate total length for females reaching up to 25 centimeters [Li = up to 25 centimeters]. This sexually dimorphic trait is measured from the snout to the tip of the tail and represents the maximum recorded size for adult females in the species. The ultimate wet weight for females is approximately 42 grams [Wwi = approximately 42 grams], though body mass can vary substantially depending on nutritional status and reproductive condition, with some gravid individuals reportedly achieving weights between 50 and 70 grams. This asymptotic mass is typically reached after several years of steady growth and is sustained through the reproductively active adult stage. The relatively modest adult size of Correlophus ciliatus compared to other diplodactylid geckos is thought to be an adaptation to its arboreal, insectivorous niche in the humid forests of New Caledonia.

Reproductive activity in the Crested gecko follows a distinct seasonal pattern when maintained under controlled captive conditions at 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. Females produce clutches containing a consistent litter size of 2 young per clutch [N_R_i = 2 young per clutch], a fixed number that appears to be evolutionarily conserved within this lineage. The interval between successive clutches during the breeding cycle is typically 4 to 6 weeks [F_R_i = 4 to 6 weeks], and this breeding activity extends across a period of 8 to 10 months. This relatively slow reproductive pace, when combined with the small clutch size, results in a modest annual reproductive output that is typical of a K-selected life history strategy. The extended inter-clutch interval likely allows the female sufficient time to replenish the energetic reserves required for vitellogenesis and egg production following each oviposition event.

Puberty in Correlophus ciliatus is not reached until well after the first year of life when the animals are maintained under stable thermal conditions. Specifically, the time since birth at puberty is approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days] at a rearing temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. This extended pre-reproductive juvenile period is characterized by continued somatic growth and the gradual onset of gonadal maturation. The attainment of sexual maturity is marked by the first successful copulation and subsequent egg production in females, though first reproduction may occur slightly later than the physiological onset of puberty. This developmental timeline is consistent with that of other arboreal geckos in the genus Correlophus, which are known for their relatively slow maturation rates compared to many smaller-bodied gekkonids.

The lifespan of the Crested gecko under captive conditions is notably long for a reptile of its body size. When animals are maintained at a constant temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the maximum recorded longevity is approximately 17.5 years [am = approximately 17.5 years]. Some individuals have been documented to live between 15 and 20 years [am = between 15 and 20 years] in optimal captive environments at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with late sexual maturation and low annual fecundity, positions Correlophus ciliatus as a slow-living species with a life history strategy geared toward high adult survival rather than high reproductive output. Such extended longevity is relatively common among New Caledonian geckos, which inhabit a relatively stable, predator-depauperate island ecosystem where the benefits of iteroparity over many reproductive seasons outweigh the advantages of rapid, early reproduction. Natural mortality in the wild is likely driven by senescence and age-related physiological deterioration rather than by intense predation pressure.
